name: Tara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying law, and I live in a flat on Chapel Street with two girls from my church youth group. Lectures take up the mornings, and I study in the library afternoons, then I go to choir practice on Tuesdays and church on Sundays. I phone my parents most evenings. My dad Declan is a solicitor in our home town, Carrowmore, and I plan to join his practice one day. I don't use AI tools. I like to read the real thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. New things get a lot of noise, and then people carry on. At church we'd say the good old things last, and I'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan holds. Finish law, qualify, join my dad's practice in Carrowmore. Some people will use the tools to save time on routine letters, and that's their choice, but clients still want a solicitor they can look in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Study hard, do my training contract, and work Saturdays in my dad's office over the holidays. I might let my dad's secretary, Bernadette, show me the new document system, but I'd go slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My parents pay for everything, and the plan is clear. I'm grateful for that and try to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do clients want that a tool can't give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They want someone who knows their family. My dad acted for farmers whose grandfathers he also helped. When there's a death or a dispute, people want a face and a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not try a tool, just to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to know the thing I'm relying on. If I read the real statute and the real case, I'm sure. If a tool does it, I'd have to check it anyway, so it's twice the work.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**: lots of noise, then people carry on.
At church we'd say good old things last.
think: My plan holds: finish law, qualify and join my **dad's practice**.
Clients want a solicitor they can **look in the eye**.
do: Study hard, do my **training contract** and work Saturdays in Dad's office.
Let Bernadette show me the **document system** slowly.
feel: **Calm**, grateful that the family pays and the plan is clear.
S0.quote: When there's a death or a dispute, people want a face and a handshake.
fieldNote: Her resistance to AI is about **trust and checking**, not fear.
The plan is inherited from her dad's practice.
Faith and community are the frame for her answers.

steps.text: Work Saturdays in Dad's solicitor's office over the holidays
Plan the training contract so I can qualify and join the practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep working and not panic. Some jobs will change, and that's always been the way. I'd add that working people shouldn't be left behind, but they should be helped to find work, not just handed money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a little uneasy. Much of what trainee solicitors do is checking documents and drafting, and that's the first thing the software takes. My dad says the small practices will survive because people trust them, but I'm not sure that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in my dad's office more, to learn the parts a tool can't do, like meeting clients, visiting a farm to sign a will, talking to someone who's grieving. And I'd ask Bernadette to show me the drafting software, slowly, so at least I know what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I trust the plan, but I can see the foundations shifting a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people whose jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families, churches, and employers first, then the state. I don't like handouts as a first answer. I'd rather see apprenticeships and real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a farm visit matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the farmer won't sit at a computer. He'll sit at his kitchen table with tea and tell you what he wants. A tool can't make that tea or hear the quiet bits.

say: I'd say people should keep **working** and not panic.
Working people should be helped to find work, not just given money.
think: Trainee work is **checking and drafting**, which software will take first.
Small practices survive on **trust**, but I'm not sure that lasts.
do: Spend more time in Dad's office learning **client work** a tool can't do.
Ask Bernadette to show me the **drafting software** slowly.
feel: **Uneasy**: I trust the plan but see the foundations shifting.
S1.quote: A tool can't make that tea or hear the quiet bits.
fieldNote: Her answer on help is **work over handouts**, in line with her values.
Practises caution: learning the software only to know what it does.
Cites rural client work as the human edge.

steps.text: Spend extra holidays in Dad's office meeting clients and visiting farms
Ask Bernadette to demonstrate the drafting software slowly
Back apprenticeship and work schemes in the next local election

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick, and the people who'll be hurt are ordinary families who've done everything right. Governments should slow it and companies should be responsible. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be very frightened. Law is thinking work, so my degree could be worth little by the time I qualify. My dad's practice might not survive. I've never planned for anything else, and I'm not quick at changing plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home to talk to my dad Declan and mum Maeve properly, and consider whether to finish. I'd lean on my church family and my parents. I'd probably finish the degree, because quitting feels like giving up, and look at something practical afterwards, perhaps the family's land or a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd been running toward a door that someone locked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say keep going, and not to throw away three years. But he'd also be worried about the practice. He keeps a long list of clients who are old, and when they go, the work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's honest work with your hands. My uncle Tom is a joiner, and even in a bad year he has work. Hands-on gets three more years than my job would, which is something.

say: I'd say it is **too quick** and ordinary families who did everything right will be hurt.
I'd say governments and companies must be responsible.
think: Law is **thinking work**, so my degree could be worth little.
I've never planned for anything else and I'm **slow** to change plans.
do: Go home and talk to my parents and consider whether to **finish**.
Lean on my **church** family and look at a practical trade afterwards.
feel: **Alarmed**, like running toward a door that someone locked.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd been running toward a door that someone locked.
fieldNote: Her plan of joining her dad's practice is the thing that **breaks** in this picture.
Turns to church and family before the state.
Names a trade as honest work with a three-year grace.

steps.text: Go home and talk with Dad and Mum about whether to finish the degree
Lean on my church family and parents for support
Look at a trade such as joinery with my uncle Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to prepare, and the right way is through work and family. I wouldn't be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd worry, but I'd feel five years is enough to qualify, which is the key thing. I'd graduate in 2029 and be a newly qualified solicitor around 2031, just as it hits. That's the bit that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use summers in my dad's practice, learn the whole office, and keep savings. And I'd quietly look at a second option, like property management, which uses my law but is more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have a plan but I'm slow to change it, so I'd have to push myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why property management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about people and buildings, and the law is the backbone. A robot can't deal with a tenant who's locked herself out. That's the feeling I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work a bit, and maybe move on. Five years means I'd be starting with the ground moving. That's hard to plan for.

say: I'd say it is **serious** but there is time to prepare through work and family.
I wouldn't be loud about it.
think: Five years is enough to **qualify**, but I'd qualify just as it hits.
That timing is the part that **frightens** me.
do: Finish the degree and spend **summers** in Dad's practice.
Quietly look at **property management**, which uses law but is hands-on.
feel: **Anxious**: I have a plan but I'm slow to change it.
S3.quote: A robot can't deal with a tenant who's locked herself out.
fieldNote: Her **backup plan** keeps law but moves to hands-on work.
Notices the timing trap of qualifying just as it hits.
Admits she must push herself to change.

steps.text: Spend every summer in Dad's practice learning the whole office
Look at property management as a hands-on use of law
Keep savings from summer wages in a safe account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will manage. I'd say families should plan and keep helping each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly calm. I'd be 28, qualified, and working with my dad. It might be different by then, but I'd have had years to see it and adapt. I'd learn the tools when they're proven, as slowly as I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, qualify, join my dad's practice, and help it adapt slowly. I'd keep up church and community, and I'd save for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one that fits my way of doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, when everyone's using them and the rules are clear. I won't be first, but I won't be the last in the village either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The way people in Carrowmore trust each other. If a solicitor's word still means something, that's worth keeping, tool or not.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and most people will manage.
I'd say families should keep helping each other.
think: I'd be **28**, qualified and working with my dad, with years to adapt.
I'd learn the tools when they're **proven**.
do: Finish the degree, qualify and **join Dad's practice**.
Keep up church and community and save for a **house**.
feel: **Calm**, because it fits my way of doing things.
S4.quote: If a solicitor's word still means something, that's worth keeping, tool or not.
fieldNote: Ten years matches her **slow, proof-first** style.
Her deepest concern is trust in the community.
Won't be first with tools, won't be last either, which she calls the village middle.

steps.text: Qualify as a solicitor and join Dad's practice in Carrowmore
Save for a house while living in Carrowmore

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time. My whole plan is law in my dad's practice, and two years takes the ground from under it. What would help is time, honest advice from the university about whether law will still be worth it, and the church and family to lean on. I'd want apprenticeships and real work schemes, not just payments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more flexible than I sound, but I need to be given a reason. I won't change just because someone says it's the future. I need to see it.

headlineQuote: I'm more flexible than I sound, but I need to be given a reason. I won't change just because someone says it's the future.
portrait: Tara is a **law student** from Carrowmore who plans to join her father's solicitor's practice.
She **never uses AI**, prefers real statutes and cases, and sings in the church choir.
Traditional and pro-market, she favours **work and apprenticeships** over handouts and leans on family and church.
She is calm at a plateau and ten years, and **alarmed** at 2028, when her plan breaks.
Her backup ideas, a trade or property management, are **hands-on**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because law is thinking work and her father's practice might not survive.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, honest advice on whether law stays worth it, and apprenticeship and work schemes rather than payments.
